name: Vendor Assessment
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Reading the Fine Print: Assessing Blockchain Vendors and Platforms
lesson.summary: Choosing a blockchain platform or vendor is as much a governance and exit-strategy decision as a technical one, since the biggest long-term risk is usually lock-in to a platform or provider you can no longer leave.
lesson.body:
Once a technology evaluation concludes that some form of blockchain is genuinely warranted, a second, distinct decision follows: which platform, and whose implementation of it. This is where vendor lock-in, introduced earlier in the course as a general risk of depending on a single supplier's proprietary technology, becomes concrete and consequential, because blockchain platforms vary enormously in how easy they are to leave once you have committed to them.

A useful vendor assessment starts by separating the platform from the provider. Is the underlying software open source, like Hyperledger Fabric or Ethereum-derived enterprise chains, where the code itself is available regardless of which vendor helped you deploy it, or is it a proprietary blockchain-as-a-service offering built and controlled by a single cloud provider, where switching means rewriting your application against a different, incompatible system entirely? Open source does not eliminate lock-in risk on its own, since a heavily customized deployment can still be practically hard to migrate, but it changes the nature of the risk from being trapped by a single company's business decisions to being trapped by your own integration choices, which are at least within your control to manage.

Beyond that structural question, a serious vendor assessment should examine data portability and exit mechanics explicitly, and concretely: if the relationship ended tomorrow, could you export the ledger's full history in a usable, verifiable format, or does the provider control the only copy in a form only their tooling can read? It should look at the health and independence of the governance around the platform itself, distinct from the consortium governance covered earlier in this course; a platform steered by a broad, multi-organization foundation behaves differently over time than one controlled unilaterally by its original vendor, who may deprioritize it, change its licensing terms, or be acquired. And it should price total cost of ownership honestly, including integration effort, the specialized talent required to operate the platform, and support contract costs, rather than comparing vendors on licensing fees alone, since licensing is often the smallest line item in an enterprise blockchain deployment.

A concrete way to see the trade-off is comparing two real paths to the same permissioned network: self-hosting an open-source Hyperledger Fabric deployment on your own infrastructure, versus buying a managed blockchain-as-a-service product from a single cloud vendor that handles node operation for you. The managed option is faster to stand up and requires less specialized in-house talent, a genuine and often decisive advantage for a resource-constrained pilot. The self-hosted option costs more in operational effort up front but preserves the ability to migrate providers, renegotiate terms, or bring operations in-house later without rewriting the application layer. Neither choice is universally correct; the right one depends on how much the organization values speed now against flexibility later, which is exactly the kind of trade-off the technology evaluation framework from earlier in this course is built to make explicit rather than leaving it as an unexamined default.
